entries.clue: Doubt integrity of Detective Inspectors given time to decline (8)

blocks.note: a Detective Inspector is a DI in the British police, and the clue asks for more than one of them
t is the standard abbreviation for time, the one physics puts in its equations
skills left unused are said to rust, which is to fall away by degrees

annotation.surface: Wondering whether a pair of police detectives can be trusted once their careers have been left to go to seed.
annotation.walkthrough: The clue's own subject is police honesty, so the opening words sound like part of that story rather than the definition. British ranks hand crosswords DI, DS and DC, all worth learning.
annotation.definitionFit: To distrust a thing is to doubt that it is honest or sound, which is to doubt its integrity.

entries.clue: Leaves those fighting Britain in protests (6)

indicatorNotes.in: What is in a thing sits inside it, so this letter is planted within the word that follows.

blocks.note: a demo is a protest march, and the clue wants a plural of them
B is the usual single letter standing for Britain

annotation.surface: Enemies of Britain carrying their fight onto the streets in a wave of demonstrations.
annotation.walkthrough: At the end of a war the forces are demobilised: uniforms handed back, men sent home on what the army itself calls demob leave. The marching in the surface is a different kind of crowd altogether.
annotation.definitionFit: Demob is the discharge of service personnel when a war ends, granting final leave to the people who have been doing the fighting.

entries.clue: Dines in haste; expresses derision (6)

blocks.note: eating fast and greedily, the blunt British slang verb for wolfing a meal down
jeering openly, the verb you do at somebody's expense

annotation.surface: Somebody gulping a meal down while sneering at what is on the plate.
annotation.walkthrough: The semicolon is the only join, and it invites you to read one sentence about a rude diner. The eating sense is slang — the same word is a noun meaning food — while the jeering sense is plain English.
annotation.definitionFit: Scoff is both the slang verb for bolting a meal down and the ordinary verb for jeering, so each half of the clue is a straight synonym.

entries.clue: Once again, tries overseeing a Latin band's practice? (9)

indicatorNotes.overseeing: To oversee is to stand above and look down, so in a down entry these letters sit on top of the ones that follow.

blocks.note: the prefix that puts again in front of a verb — redo, retake, rerun
a judge who tries a case hears it, so the court's two verbs are interchangeable
the article taken down exactly as it stands
L is the dictionary's label on a word borrowed from Latin

annotation.surface: Another go at supervising a Latin band while they practise their set.
annotation.walkthrough: The courtroom sense of 'tries' is the piece to spot, and 'Once again' looks like it belongs to the trying rather than to the letters. The question mark admits that a band's practice is only one instance of the thing.
annotation.definitionFit: A rehearsal is any run-through held before the performance, and a band's practice is one example of it, which is what the question mark marks.

entries.clue: Marries striker that's playing in PM (3,4,7)

indicatorNotes.playing: A loose part in a machine is said to have play in it, moving freely instead of staying put, so these letters need not keep their order.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, fourteen letters

annotation.surface: A centre forward who turns out in the afternoons getting married.
annotation.walkthrough: 'PM' is the two-letter afternoon in the surface and the office in the definition. Sir Keir Starmer led Labour from 2020 and became Prime Minister in July 2024; the knighthood is what makes the enumeration start at three.
annotation.definitionFit: Sir Keir Starmer has been Britain's Prime Minister since July 2024, so PM names by office the man the letters spell.

entries.clue: Composer Lionel, taking starters, accrues bumper charges for refreshments (3,3)

indicatorNotes.taking starters: A starter is whatever comes first, so what is taken is the opening letter of each word that follows.

blocks.note: Lionel Bart, who wrote the songs for the musical Oliver!
the opening letter of each of these two words

annotation.surface: A composer ordering first courses and running up an enormous bill for food and drink.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Starters' is the pivot: the surface orders a first course while the wordplay collects opening letters. Bumper means nothing more than very large, as in a bumper crop, and the surname is hiding behind a first name.
annotation.definitionFit: A bar tab is the running account a drinker builds up over an evening and settles at the end — the charges for what has been served.

entries.clue: Hairy Evans regularly shaved sections (5)

indicatorNotes.regularly shaved: Something shaved at regular intervals loses every other letter, so only the ones in the even positions are left standing.

blocks.note: the two words read as one run, keeping the second letter, then the fourth, and so on to the end

annotation.surface: A hirsute man named Evans who keeps to a shaving routine.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Shaved' belongs to the hairy Evans of the surface and to the letters being stripped out, which is the whole of the joke. Counting starts at the second letter here, not the first — Everyman uses both.
annotation.definitionFit: An area is a stretch or part of something, as in the areas of a report or of a city, so the plural covers sections.

entries.clue: Airtight container for gunpowder? (3,5)

blocks.note: read as the sealed magazine where an explosive is kept dry, and meant as the little lidded box on the kitchen shelf
Gunpowder is a Chinese green tea whose leaves are rolled into hard pellets that look like grains of shot

annotation.surface: A sealed box for keeping explosive powder safely dry.
annotation.walkthrough: The trap is that gunpowder reads as the explosive and there is nothing else in the clue to argue with it. The question mark is the setter conceding that one particular tea is standing in for all of them.
annotation.definitionFit: A caddy is the small airtight box tea is stored in, and Gunpowder is one of the teas that would go in it, so the clue describes the thing straight.

entries.clue: Tormentor going round southeast Spain? 'Correct!' (5-3)

indicatorNotes.going round: To go round a thing is to close about it, so the letters in front open up and take the next ones inside.

blocks.note: the one in the playground who makes another child's life a misery
the compass point in its usual two letters
E is Spain's international vehicle code, from España — the oval sticker on the back of a Spanish car

annotation.surface: A playground bully touring the southeastern corner of Spain.
annotation.walkthrough: The exclamation at the end is the definition, which is easy to read as the last word of the surface story instead. The question mark after Spain flags the country standing in for its one-letter code.
annotation.definitionFit: Bulls-eye is what you shout when somebody has hit the dead centre of the target, and so when they have got a thing exactly right.

entries.clue: Tale that ends with a sentence? (9,5)

annotation.definition: Tale that ends with a sentence?

blocks.note: read as any story at all, since every story ends somewhere — the surface gives no hint which kind is meant
on the surface the last string of words on the page; in the answer the term handed down from the bench once the verdict is in

annotation.surface: A story whose closing words are, inevitably, a sentence.
annotation.walkthrough: Read one way the clue says nothing at all — every tale ends with a sentence — and that flatness is what hides the second sense. The sentence that matters is passed by a judge.
annotation.definitionFit: A courtroom drama is the trial story as a genre, built to run all the way to the verdict and the sentencing that closes it.

entries.clue: Bum, low singer (7)

blocks.note: to low is what cattle do, and this is the noise written out
the American singer of Believe, who goes by one name only

annotation.surface: A shabby performer with a voice down in the cellar.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Low' looks like a register and is the cattle's verb. A pop star with a single name is a gift to setters, because the whole of her goes into the grid without an initial to explain.
annotation.definitionFit: To mooch is to drift about cadging from people, so a moocher is a bum in the American sense of an idle sponger.

entries.clue: Blanket and protective garment cut short (7)

indicatorNotes.cut short: Something cut short loses its end, so the last letter of the word just named never arrives.

blocks.note: the loose boiler suit a mechanic pulls on over their clothes is named in the plural, and the instruction alongside docks its final S

annotation.surface: Bedding and workwear, both of them trimmed down.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Blanket' is the adjective, not the bedding: a blanket ban is one that covers every case without exception, and that is the sense the answer carries.
annotation.definitionFit: A blanket ban and an overall ban are the same thing, both adjectives meaning applying to everything without exception.

entries.clue: Acronym's 'Best Actresses' for Thora aplenty! (5)

indicatorNotes.Acronym's: An acronym is built from the opening letter of each word it stands for, so only the initials of what follows are wanted.

blocks.note: the first letter of each of these five words in turn

annotation.surface: An actress collecting award after award for her leading performances.
annotation.walkthrough: The whole sentence defines and the whole sentence is the wordplay. Thora Hird was the Lancashire actress of Last of the Summer Wine and Alan Bennett's Talking Heads, and she took the best-actress television award twice.
annotation.definitionFit: Read straight, the clue is about the British film and television academy, whose Best Actress awards Thora Hird collected more than once.

entries.clue: Old Italians, recusants undergoing reform (9)

indicatorNotes.undergoing reform: To reform a thing is to form it again in a different shape, so these letters are made up afresh.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, nine letters

annotation.surface: Refusers of the state church being brought into line during the Reformation.
annotation.walkthrough: Recusants were the English Catholics who would not attend Anglican services after the Reformation, which is why 'reform' sits so comfortably beside them. The Etruscans held central Italy before Rome swallowed them.
annotation.definitionFit: The Etruscans were the people of Etruria in central Italy, flourishing there for centuries before Rome absorbed them — old Italians exactly.

entries.clue: In a flap, I fled nursery? Understandable (4-8)

indicatorNotes.In a flap: Somebody in a flap is panicking and all over the place, so the letters beside it are in no settled order.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, twelve letters

annotation.surface: A small child in a panic bolting away from playgroup.
annotation.walkthrough: Everyman's anagram signals are nearly always states of agitation — in a flap, at sea, upset — and the question mark marks the flight as a supposition rather than a fact.
annotation.definitionFit: Something user-friendly is built so an ordinary person can work it out without help, which is to say it is understandable.

entries.clue: Endearing, mercurial, deep-rooted (9)

indicatorNotes.mercurial: A mercurial temper changes from one moment to the next, so the letters it describes will not hold the arrangement they came in.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, nine letters

annotation.surface: A character sketch of someone lovable, changeable and set in their ways.
annotation.walkthrough: Three adjectives in a row and only the middle one is an instruction. Mercury the liquid metal runs away from anything that tries to hold it, which is where a mercurial person gets the name.
annotation.definitionFit: An engrained habit has worked so far into the grain that it cannot be got out again, which is what deep-rooted describes.

entries.clue: Divorcée in resort became frosty (4,4)

indicatorNotes.in resort: To re-sort is to sort a second time into a different order, and that is what 'in resort' is asking of the letters beside it.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, eight letters, the accent counting for nothing

annotation.surface: A newly single woman at a seaside town turning cold towards everybody.
annotation.walkthrough: 'In resort' looks like a place and is really re-sort, one of the quieter anagram signals. The accent on the fodder is there for the surface alone and never reaches the grid.
annotation.definitionFit: A pond or a windscreen that has iced over has gone from clear to frozen, which is what becoming frosty amounts to.

entries.clue: Less tidy, in a way - but with a distinct character (8)

indicatorNotes.in a way: 'In a way' means in one manner among several, so the letters beside it are to be set down in some order other than the given one.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, eight letters

annotation.surface: A room messier than it was, though it has a character all of its own.
annotation.walkthrough: The dash invites you to take 'Less tidy, in a way' as one judgement and move on; it is fodder and instruction sitting side by side. Stylised art drops realism for a deliberate manner.
annotation.definitionFit: A stylised drawing or gesture is done in a set, deliberate manner rather than naturally, so it carries a character distinctly its own.

entries.clue: Hack takes in tipsy tattler where farmer offers drink (6,6)

indicatorNotes.takes in: To take something in is to receive it inside, so the word in front opens up to admit the letters that follow.
indicatorNotes.tipsy: Somebody tipsy is unsteady on their feet, so the letters described that way will not stand in the order given.

blocks.note: a hack is the dry rasping bark of a smoker clearing his chest
a tattler is a tell-tale, and these seven letters go inside once they have been shaken up

annotation.surface: A journalist listening hard to a drunk who is giving the whole story away.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Hack' is the journalist the surface wants and the smoker's cough the wordplay needs, and a tell-tale is exactly who such a journalist would be buying drinks for. The definition describes the thing rather than naming it.
annotation.definitionFit: A cattle trough is the long water container standing in a field, which is where a farmer sets drink out for the herd.

entries.clue: Increasingly feeble wordplay Everyman offered with hesitant expression (6)

blocks.note: the joke that turns on one word carrying two senses at once
Everyman is the name this setter signs his puzzles with, so he can speak of himself in the first person
the noise made while casting about for the next word

annotation.surface: The setter owning up to jokes that get weaker as the puzzle goes on.
annotation.walkthrough: A setter naming himself in his own clue is one of the oldest habits in the craft, and the pseudonym stands in for a single letter. 'Increasingly' is what makes the definition a comparative.
annotation.definitionFit: Puny means small and weak, so its comparative describes a thing growing feebler by degrees.

entries.clue: Eschews restaurant: meat singed in parts (4,2)

indicatorNotes.in parts: Something true in parts is only partly true, so only a part of the words beside it is wanted and the rest is left behind.

blocks.note: six letters running on unbroken across the gap between the two words

annotation.surface: A restaurant given a miss because its meat comes out scorched here and there.
annotation.walkthrough: 'In parts' serves both sentences at once: the meat is burnt here and there, and only part of the words in front is being asked for. Everyman hides across a word boundary nearly every time.
annotation.definitionFit: To eat in is to have your meal at home rather than go out for it, which is to eschew the restaurant.

entries.clue: Fancy food shop, veal - not half raw - supplied (9)

indicatorNotes.not half: A word that is not half there keeps only half its letters, and it is the opening half that joins onto what comes before.

blocks.note: the counter selling cold meats, olives and other fine groceries, short for delicatessen
the opening half of the word, which is all the instruction alongside leaves standing
skin rubbed raw is left red and sore

annotation.surface: A smart grocer sending round veal that turned out to be badly underdone.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Not half' is the trap. In British speech it means the opposite of what it says — not half raw is very raw indeed — which is how the surface reads it, while the wordplay takes it literally and removes half a word.
annotation.definitionFit: Goods that have been delivered have been brought round and handed over, which is to say supplied.

entries.clue: Victory: rebuffed a tailless big cat: ta-da! (5)

indicatorNotes.rebuffed: To rebuff is to push a thing back the way it came, so these letters are set down from the end.
indicatorNotes.tailless: An animal with no tail has lost its last part, so the final letter of the word goes.

blocks.note: V for victory, the sign Churchill made with two fingers
the article in front of a lion, the lion docked of its last letter, and the four of them written out backwards

annotation.surface: A triumphant announcement that a big cat with no tail has been seen off.
annotation.walkthrough: The two colons make the clue read like a caption under a photograph, which hides where the definition starts. A big cat with no tail is an instruction to drop a letter, not a fact about the animal.
annotation.definitionFit: Voila is the French flourish English has borrowed for presenting a result — there it is — which is the job ta-da does.

entries.clue: Polish entering AA somewhere in the Antilles (5)

indicatorNotes.entering: What enters a thing goes inside it, so these letters are set within the pair that follows.

blocks.note: the two letters are taken from the clue exactly as they stand
to polish a surface is to rub it, the verb hiding behind the capital letter

annotation.surface: A Pole signing up for Alcoholics Anonymous.
annotation.walkthrough: The capital P is the whole trick: it looks like the nationality and is the verb. AA reads as the meeting, or as Britain's motoring organisation, and is only ever two letters here.
annotation.definitionFit: Aruba is a small Dutch island off the coast of Venezuela, one of the Lesser Antilles in the Caribbean.

entries.clue: Gleaned from harvest? I get just a trace (7)

indicatorNotes.Gleaned from: To glean is to pick up the few ears left lying in a field after the reapers have gone, so a handful of letters is picked out of what follows.

blocks.note: seven letters running on unbroken from the middle of the first word, with the question mark counting for nothing

annotation.surface: Somebody complaining that the harvest has left them next to nothing.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Gleaned from harvest' is the instruction and the picture at once, since gleaners took only what the reapers had left. The question mark sits inside the run of letters, which is as good a hiding place as punctuation offers.
annotation.definitionFit: A vestige is the small surviving remnant of something that has otherwise gone, so it amounts to just a trace of it.

entries.clue: Drop of alcohol loosens up relatives (7)

indicatorNotes.Drop of: A drop is the smallest measure a liquid comes in, so only the opening letter of the word after it is taken.

blocks.note: the opening letter of the word, which is all a drop amounts to
to loosen a knot up is to undo it

annotation.surface: A small drink making the family relax at a gathering.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Drop of' is the giveaway: an amount that small can only be one letter, and it is the one the word starts with. The surface's drink is what loosens the knot as well.
annotation.definitionFit: Aunties are your parents' sisters, so the plural names relatives directly, in the affectionate form rather than the formal one.

entries.clue: Give another hand to leader needing attention (6)

indicatorNotes.needing attention: A thing needing attention is not in the state it should be and has to be put right, so these letters are rearranged.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, six letters

annotation.surface: Lending a hand to a boss who is struggling and needs looking after.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Give another hand to' reads as an offer of help, and the hand is the card player's. At the table a misdeal or a dispute is followed by precisely this.
annotation.definitionFit: To redeal is to deal the pack out again from the start, which is to give every player another hand.

entries.clue: Bureaucrat: one of five daily? (8)

blocks.note: the senior civil servant running a government department, a Whitehall figure rather than a clerk
five-a-day is the British health campaign's target of five portions of fruit and vegetables, and a small loose-skinned citrus counts as one of them

annotation.surface: An official who turns out to be one of a daily five.
annotation.walkthrough: The second definition is the fruit, and 'five daily' has to be heard as the health campaign's slogan before it means anything. The question mark concedes that the fruit is only an example of a portion.
annotation.definitionFit: A mandarin is the senior civil servant at the head of a department, and also the small loose-skinned orange that counts as one portion towards five a day.
